food.text: A 10th-century Arabic cookbook describes two types of kashk. One was made of wheat and leaven, and the other of sour milk. The same word covered very different foods, from a grain-based dish to a dairy one.

In the 10th-century Persian Shahnameh, or Book of Kings, Firdausi uses the word kashk to mean barley flour. Today the word is better known for a dried dairy product, so its meaning has changed a great deal over the centuries.

Persian-Arabian food is described as beginning with cooking techniques innovated in ancient Persia and carried forward by Persians during the Sassanid Dynasty. The cuisine of Eastern Arabia, around the Persian Gulf, later blended Persian, Indian, Lebanese and Chinese cooking styles.
Firdausi's Shahnameh does not use kashk only for barley flour. The poem also uses the word for a mixture of cracked wheat and cracked barley, showing that kashk could be a coarse, mixed grain food.

Francoise Aubaile-Sallenave argues that the original Persian kashk known from early Persian literature was made from barley with either leaven and water or some fermented milk. She suggests that Iranian-speaking pastoralists, who relied on dried sour milk and had little barley, later applied the word to dry sour milk.

The Middle Persian text Xusraw ud rēdag mentions kashk in adjectival form, in the phrase ārd ī kaškēn. This is one of the earliest known written traces of a food word that Persian speakers still use today.

art.text: Iranian architecture developed what is called the Khorasani style from the late 7th century until the end of the 10th century CE. Examples include the Jameh Mosque of Nain and the Jameh Mosque of Isfahan. Historian Arthur Pope called architecture the supreme Iranian art.

The Hadiths prohibit eating and drinking vessels of gold and silver, which had been the ideal in ancient Rome and Persia. As a result, Muslim elites used pottery and glass for tableware. Restrictions on figurative wall painting also encouraged decorative, often geometric tiles, the most distinctive speciality of Islamic ceramics.

Early Muslim palaces had domes that blended elements of both Byzantine and Persian architecture, using both pendentives and squinches. Domed halls appeared in palaces as early as the eighth century, well before domes became standard in mosques. Early palace domes were likely used to mark the ruler's place during ceremonies.

The last time rock-relief frescoes were painted was at Taq-e Bostan, under Khosrow II, the last important Sassanid ruler. The thousand-year-old tradition did not survive the Muslim conquest of Persia in the 7th century AD.
art.source_title: Art of rock relief in ancient Iran

art.text: Domed fountains at mosques in places such as Nishapur seem to be related to an element of palace architecture. An example is the domed structure over a shallow pool at the mid-eighth-century palace of Khirbat al-Mafjar. At mosques, such fountains were later used as part of ritual ablution.

Countryside residences from this period were enclosed by outer walls with semi-circular towers. Inside they had central courtyards or a central domed hall flanked by vaulted halls. Some had four iwans flanking a central courtyard.

war.text: When Emperor Maurice was murdered by the usurper Phocas, Khosrow II declared war, claiming to avenge his benefactor. The Persians conquered much of the Levant, Egypt and even some of Anatolia. Then the resurgence of Heraclius turned the balance against them.

The Sasanians used war elephants, which terrified enemies and could break their ranks. At the Battle of al-Qādisiyyah in 636 AD, a unit of thirty-three elephants was used against the invading Arab Muslims.

The Byzantines and the Persian Sasanids had been severely weakened by a long succession of wars, especially the climactic war of 602-628. Under Umar, the second Caliph, the Muslims decisively conquered Syria and Mesopotamia and entirely toppled the Sasanids.

In mid-September 627, Heraclius launched a surprising and risky winter invasion of Sasanian Mesopotamia. At the Battle of Nineveh, 6,000 Persians fell after eight hours of fighting. Nikephoros says Rhahzadh, the Sasanian commander, challenged Heraclius to single combat and was killed by him in a single thrust, though doubt has been cast on this; in any case Rhahzadh died during the battle and his remaining forces retreated. It was the climactic battle of the Byzantine-Sasanian War of 602-628.

Under the peace treaty, the Byzantines regained all their lost territories, their captured soldiers and a war indemnity. They also recovered the True Cross and other relics lost in Jerusalem in 614. Heraclius did not impose harsh terms, knowing his own empire was near exhaustion.

In 654, the Battle of Badghis pitted the Karen family and their Hephthalite allies against the Rashidun Caliphate, led by Abd Allah ibn Amir. It completed the first phase of the Rashidun conquest of Iran.

In 900, the Samanids defeated the Alids of Tabaristan at Gorgan. The Alid leader Muhammad ibn Zayd was severely wounded and captured, and died the next day. His son was also captured, and the Samanids took control of Tabaristan.

Rhahzadh trailed Heraclius with an army of 12,000 but could not catch him. Heraclius took food and fodder from the countryside, so Rhahzadh marched through stripped land and struggled to feed his soldiers and animals. Heraclius' Göktürk allies also deserted him because of the strange winter conditions.

After the defeat, the Persian army rebelled and overthrew Khosrow II, raising his son Kavad II in his place. Khosrow perished in a dungeon after suffering for five days on bare sustenance, and on the fifth day he was shot slowly to death with arrows. Kavad at once sent peace offers to Heraclius.
Hurqus ibn Zuhayr was a key Arab commander in the conquest of Persia. In 638 the Rashidun army sent him to defeat Hormuzan at Ahvaz. He forced the city to pay jizya, a poll-tax.
In 901, the Persian Samanids defeated Amr Saffari at the battle of Balkh. The defeat reduced the Saffarid dynasty to a minor tributary in Sistan.

After Muhammad ibn Zayd died, his corpse was decapitated. His head was sent to the Samanid court at Bukhara and his body was buried at the gate of Gurgan. According to al-Mas'udi, his tomb soon became a centre of pilgrimage.

literature.text: The tenth-century Persian poet Ferdowsi wrote the Shahnameh, or "Book of Kings", the national epic of Iran. It is mostly based on the Xwadāynāmag, a Middle Persian compilation of the history of Iranian kings and heroes, along with Zoroastrian stories from texts such as the Avesta.

Middle Persian was the prestige dialect of the Sasanian era, and it is the largest source of Zoroastrian literature. After the Arab conquest, Zoroastrian priests kept using it for religious and secular writings in the Aramaic-derived Book Pahlavi script. These works are traditionally known as "Pahlavi literature".

Persian literature is described as one of the great literatures of humanity, and Goethe judged it one of the four main bodies of world literature. Most of what survives comes from after the Muslim conquest of Persia around 650 CE. Its roots lie in surviving works of Middle Persian and Old Persian.

Sasanian court priests compiled an immense chronicle called the Khwaday Namag, or "Book of Kings". It was a legendary genealogy that linked the Sasanian kings to Vishtaspa, Zoroaster's patron and the legendary founder of the mythological Kayanian dynasty.

After the Abbasids came to power in 750 AD, Iranians became the scribes and bureaucrats of the Islamic Caliphate and, increasingly, its writers and poets. New Persian literature arose and flourished in Khorasan and Transoxiana, where early dynasties such as the Tahirids and Samanids were based.

The earliest Zoroastrian texts in Middle Persian were probably written down in the late Sasanian era, in the 6th and 7th centuries. They represented the codification of an earlier oral tradition rather than brand-new compositions.

After the Abbasids came to power in 750, Iranians became the scribes and bureaucrats of the Islamic Caliphate. Increasingly they also became its writers and poets. Persian speakers thus helped shape the literary life of the wider Muslim world.

A Middle Persian text called Mâdayân î chatrang, the "Book of Chess", dates from the 7th century. Its title shows how the Sanskrit word chaturanga became chatrang in Middle Persian. The book is dated to about 620 CE in the article on shatranj.
Middle Persian later produced a number of literary works centered in Manichaean and Zoroastrian religious books. These were written between the 3rd and the 10th century AD.

The original Middle Persian Khwaday Namag has been lost. Its contents survive only through Arabic translations and through the versified New Persian Shahnameh by Firdausi, finished around 1000. The Sasanian priests' chronicle thus lives on in a later poem.

New Persian literature arose and flourished in Khorasan and Transoxiana. The reason was political: early Iranian dynasties of post-Islamic Iran, such as the Tahirids and Samanids, were based in Khorasan.

The Mâdayân î chatrang told how the Sasanian king Khosrau I received a gift from an Indian king: a chess game with sixteen emerald and sixteen ruby pieces. It came with a challenge, which Khosrau's courtiers successfully resolved. Ferdowsi's Shahnama, around 1010, also mentions the incident.
After the Islamic conquest of Persia, shatranj spread westwards. From the 8th century onwards a considerable body of literature on game tactics and strategy was produced about it.
The earliest listing of works on chess is in the Fihrist, a general bibliography produced in 377 AH (988 AD) by Ibn al-Nadim. It devotes an entire section to the topic of chess.

Most Middle Persian texts, including the Zend commentaries and translations of the Zoroastrian canon, date from the 9th to the 11th century. By then Middle Persian had long ceased to be a spoken language. The surviving manuscripts are usually 14th-century copies.

science.text: In the Sasanian Empire, great attention was given to mathematics and astronomy, and the Academy of Gondishapur is a prominent example. Sassanid observatories were later imitated by Muslim astronomers and astrologers of the Islamic Golden Age.

In the Early Middle Ages, Persia became a stronghold of Islamic science. After the establishment of the Umayyad and Abbasid states, many Iranian scholars were sent to the capitals of these Islamic dynasties.

The 9th century mathematician Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi founded algebra and expanded upon Persian and Indian arithmetic systems. His writings were translated into Latin by Gerard of Cremona and Robert of Chester, and they influenced the development of mathematical thought in the medieval West.
In the tenth century, the Persian astronomer Abd al-Rahman al-Sufi recorded the first known reference to the Andromeda galaxy. He called it a "little cloud".
The horizontal or panemone windmill first appeared in Greater Iran during the 9th century. Windwheels had earlier been developed by the Babylonians around 1700 BC to pump water for irrigation.

The Banū Mūsā brothers were three 9th-century Persian scholars who lived and worked in Baghdad. They are known for their Book of Ingenious Devices on automata and mechanical devices, and their Book on the Measurement of Plane and Spherical Figures.

Caliph Al-Mansur instructed Ibrahim al-Fazari and Yaqub ibn Tariq to translate Brahmagupta's texts, the Brahmasphutasiddhanta and Khandakhadyaka. The translations, named Sindhind and Arkand, introduced the concept of Indian numerals to the Islamic world.

Under the Samanids, who promoted the arts and gave rise to the advancement of science and literature, scholars such as Rudaki and Avicenna were attracted to their realm. Bukhara, under Samanid control, was a rival to Baghdad in its glory.

Adolf Fonahn's 1910 work on Persian medicine lists over 400 medical works written in the Persian language, not counting authors such as Avicenna who wrote in Arabic. Historians have also recorded at least 80 oculists who wrote treatises related to ophthalmology from the beginning of 800 AD onward.

Persian astronomical tables influenced by Indian astronomy, called Zig-I shahriyarr, were translated into Arabic as Zijashshahriyar. The Abbasid leaders in Baghdad had turned to India and Persia for advanced knowledge in astronomy, mathematics and medicine.
Al-Khwarizmi, a ninth-century scholar who learned Sanskrit, played a pivotal role in spreading the Indian numeral system. Another contemporary scholar, al-Kindi, wrote four books on Indian numerals.

After the Muslim conquest, Persian scholars were deeply concerned because knowledge in the fields of science had been lost when Muslim armies destroyed major libraries. Persian literature was then translated into Arabic for approximately two centuries to preserve the surviving works.

politics.text: Between 633 and 651 CE, the Rashidun Caliphate conquered the Sasanian Empire as part of the early Muslim conquests. Persia was already facing significant political, economic and social challenges, and its army had been heavily strained by the Byzantine–Sasanian War of 602–628.

In 651, Yazdegerd III, the last Sassanid emperor, was killed near Merv by a local miller for his purse. His death put an end to both his dynasty and to organized Persian resistance. After the rest of his army was defeated at the Battle of Oxus River, he had narrowly escaped to China, according to the article, before his killing.

By the early 10th century, the Abbasids almost lost control to the Iranian Buyid dynasty (934–1062). Since much of the Abbasid administration had been Persian, the Buyids were quietly able to assume real power in Baghdad.

Hormuzan, one of the seven great chiefs of Persia, made peace treaties with Muslim commanders and broke them more than once. After Yazdegerd III sent fresh troops in late 640, Hormuzan was defeated at Tuster, captured and sent to Umar in Medina. He apparently converted to Islam and became Umar's adviser, but after Umar's assassination in November 644 he was killed by Umar's son Ubayd Allah, who claimed to have seen him conspiring with the killer while holding the murder weapon.

During Khosrow II's rule in 590–628, Egypt, Jordan, Palestine and Lebanon were annexed to the Sasanian Empire. The Sassanians called their empire Erânshahr, meaning Dominion of the Aryans, that is, of Iranians.
In 977, Sabuktigin, a Turkic governor of the Samanids, conquered Ghazna in present-day Afghanistan. He established the Ghaznavid dynasty, which lasted until 1186.

The Khurramites were a 9th-century religious and political movement based on the 8th-century teachings of Sunpadh, who preached a syncretism of Shia Islam and Zoroastrianism. Under Babak Khorramdin, the movement sought the redistribution of private wealth and the abolition of Islam.

Hormuzan apparently converted to Islam and remained a useful adviser to Umar throughout the rest of the Persian campaign. He is also believed to be the mastermind behind Umar's assassination in 644. Umar was killed by an Iranian slave, Abu Lu'lu'a Firuz, and afterwards Umar's son Ubayd Allah killed Hurmuzan, acting on a claim that he had been seen conspiring with Abu Lu'lu'a while holding the murder weapon.

Under Caliph Uthman ibn Affan, almost the whole of the former Sassanid territory rebelled from time to time, and he had to send several military expeditions to crush the rebellions and recapture Persia. The main revolts were in Armenia and Azerbaijan in 646, Fars and Sistan in 649, Makran in 650, and Khorasan in 651. In 651 Yazdegerd III, the last Sassanid emperor, was killed near Merv by a local miller for his purse, which ended his dynasty and organized Persian resistance.

Muhammad ibn Abi'l-Saj was appointed ruler of Azerbaijan in 889 or 890. As Abbasid central authority weakened toward the end of the ninth century, he formed a virtually independent state, and coins were minted in his name in 898-900.
politics.source_title: Azerbaijan in the Early Middle Ages

politics.text: In the last decade of the 10th century, the Ghaznavid empire grew by taking all of the Samanid territories south of the Amu Darya. It eventually occupied parts of Eastern Iran, Afghanistan, Pakistan and north-west India.

The Alavids were a Zaidiyyah Shia dynasty (864 to 928 AD) established in Mazandaran, in northern Iran. Later the Buyid dynasty, also Zaidiyyah Shia, emerged in Daylaman about 930 AD and extended its rule over central and western Iran and into Iraq until 1048 AD.
A genealogical list of the kings of Iran in the medieval Islamic period begins in AD 820. It notes that the Abbasid dynasty, which ruled from 750, held only brief or nominal rule from 820 onward.

philosophy.text: Under the Sasanian Empire (224–651 AD), Zoroastrianism was the main religion of Iran, but it was not alone. Manichaeanism was present, Jewish and Christian communities of the Church of the East thrived, and many people in eastern Iran, such as Bactria and Sogdia, followed Buddhism.

Arabic–Persian philosophy was strongly influenced by Ancient Greek philosophers. Its classical period began in the early 9th century CE, roughly 200 years after the death of Muhammad. Early on it focused on translating and interpreting Greek thought, and one key topic was how reason and revelation could be two compatible ways of reaching the truth.

Mazdakism was a late-5th or early-6th century proto-socialist, gnostic offshoot of Zoroastrianism. It sought to do away with private property, making it one of the boldest reform movements to grow out of Iranian religious thought.

In Zoroastrianism's oldest hymns, the Gathas, the main dualism is ethical and psychological, a choice between Asha (truth and order) and Druj (chaos and the lie). A strict cosmic dualism, with Angra Mainyu as a co-equal adversary of Ahura Mazda, is a later development prominent in Middle Persian texts like the 9th-century Bundahishn.

Zoroastrianism was the official religion of successive Iranian polities, starting with the Achaemenid Empire, which formalized many of its tenets and rituals. It ended with the Sasanian Empire, which revitalized the faith and standardized its teachings.

The Khurramites were a 9th-century religious and political movement based on the 8th century teachings of Sunpadh. They preached a syncretism of Shia Islam and Zoroastrianism, blending the new faith with older Iranian beliefs.

Islam spread only slowly among Persians after the conquest, and it was not purely voluntary. Zoroastrians were made to pay the jizya tax or be killed, enslaved or imprisoned, and the tax collectors subjected those who paid to insults and humiliation. There is evidence that Zoroastrian scriptures were burnt and Zoroastrian priests executed, particularly in areas that were centers of resistance, and the persecution drove many Zoroastrians to flee east to India. The nobility and citizens converted first, while the peasantry and the dihqans, or landed gentry, followed more slowly. By the late 10th century, the majority of Persians had become Muslim.

The early Islamic period saw the development of Persian mysticism, an interpretation of existence, life and love with Perso-Islamic Sufi monotheism as its practical aspect. It held that spiritual truth, or God, could be perceived directly through mystic practices based on divine love.
Under Babak Khorramdin, the Khurramite movement sought the redistribution of private wealth and the abolition of Islam. This gave its mix of Shia Islam and Zoroastrianism a radical social edge.

Persecution of Zoroastrians by the early Muslims in the Rashidun Caliphate prompted much of the community to migrate to the Indian subcontinent, where they were granted asylum. In cities where Arab governors lived, Zoroastrians were left with no choice but to conform to Islam or leave for regions with a more amicable administration. The poll-tax called jizya was also used to humble non-Muslims, and laws and restrictions emphasized their inferior status. The Parsis, their descendants, are thought to have been present in India since about the 9th century.

Present-day Zoroastrianism is monolithic, a continuation of the elite form of the Sasanian Empire. In antiquity, however, it had several variants or denominations, differing slightly by location, ethnic affiliation and historical period.

In the 9th-century Middle Persian text called the Bundahishn, a strict cosmic dualism appears in which Angra Mainyu (Ahriman) is a co-equal, primordial adversary of Ahura Mazda. The source describes this as a later development, not part of the early Gathas.

The Alavids dynasty (864–928 AD) became established in Mazandaran, in northern Iran, and followed Zaidiyyah Shia, sometimes called "Fiver". Around 930, the Buyid dynasty, also Zaidiyyah Shia, emerged in Daylaman and went on to extend its rule over central and western Iran.

culture.text: Between 632 and 654 AD the Rashidun Caliphate conquered Iran. Over the next two centuries of Umayyad and Abbasid rule, Iran, although initially resistant, gradually adopted Islam as its predominant faith.
The Persian Samanid dynasty made great attempts to spread the Islamic faith in the 9th and 10th centuries. At the same time it promoted a Persian cultural revival.

Although Persians adopted the religion of their conquerors, over the centuries they worked to protect and revive their distinctive language and culture. This process is known as Persianization, and Arabs and Turks participated in it.

A distinctive Turco-Persian culture arose in the 9th and 10th centuries in Khorasan and Transoxiana. Historian Robert L. Canfield describes it as Persianate because it centred on a lettered tradition of Iranian origin, and Turkic because Turkic rulers patronized it for generations.

After the Muslim conquest of Persia, Middle Persian, the language of the Sassanids, continued in wide use well into the eighth century. It served as a medium of administration in the eastern lands of the Caliphate.
